title: GPUs could explode to multiple TB with new storage-inspired memory tech
excerpt: High-bandwidth flash promises SSD-like capacities with HBM-like speeds, but it's not all unicorns and rainbows
content_html:
Virtually every high-end GPU and AI accelerator relies on high bandwidth memory (HBM), which can shuffle data around at multiple terabytes a second but can only reach into the gigabytes, with models often needing to be shared across multiple processors. However, an emerging storage technology could change that, boosting accelerator memory capacity from hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes.

The technology, called high-bandwidth flash (HBF), is being developed by Sandisk and SK Hynix and aims to provide SSD-like capacities at HBM-like speeds.

Peeling back HBF’s layers

REG AD

Conceptually, high-bandwidth flash looks and sounds a lot like HBM. It’s assembled by stacking multiple layers (16 in the case of Sandisk’s first-gen modules) of memory together, which boosts capacity and bandwidth. But where HBM uses DRAM, HBF aims to use NAND flash.

REG AD

Sandisk claims its first generation of high-bandwidth flash will supposedly achieve read bandwidths up to 1.6 TB/s [PDF], making it a bit faster than HBM3e but significantly slower than HBM4, which is already hitting 2.5 TB/s per 12-high stack. Future HBF generations are expected to push bandwidth to over 2 TB/s and eventually 3.2 TB/s.

While bandwidth makes HBF interesting as an alternative to HBM, its real party trick is capacity. Because it’s built using NAND, Sandisk says it can achieve capacities up to 256 Gb per die, which translates to 512 GB per 16-high module. That’s more than 14 times the capacity of the HBM4 used in AMD and Nvidia’s latest accelerators.

Continuing with the similarities, HBF modules share similar packaging requirements to HBM, which means you can expect them to be fused to the GPU die using advanced packaging techniques like TSMC’s CoWoS, or Intel’s EMIB and Foveros tech. Nothing particularly exotic as AI accelerators go.

What’s more, the storage vendor doesn’t expect the modules to come at a power or price premium over HBM. And from a bits per dollar standpoint, HBF looks like a stellar option. 

If all this sounds a bit too good to be true, that’s because for all of HBF’s benefits, it comes with some rather significant compromises.

NAND still isn’t DRAM

The main trade off, as we understand it, is write endurance and access latency. HBF may perform like HBM on paper, but it’s still using NAND, which has a finite write endurance before it wears out and has access latencies measured in microseconds as opposed to tens of nanoseconds for DRAM.

If you were to swap HBM for HBF, it (probably) wouldn’t perform very well and it’d wear out pretty quickly, rendering that $50,000-plus GPU of yours a paperweight — not ideal for a product that’s being asked to serve longer to suit hyperscalers' depreciation schedules.

REG AD

Instead, Sandisk and SK Hynix propose using HBF to supplement HBM to make inference more cost effective. HBM handles all the write intensive stuff while HBF takes care of the read heavy parts of the pipeline.

While we talk about inference as one job, it's really a collection of many that can broadly be broken into two categories, one that’s compute intensive and another that’s bandwidth bound.

The first of these phases, called prefill, involves tokenizing and embedding prompts, feeding them through the model in one big forward pass, generating the key value caches used to track state, and outputting the first token.

The second, called decode, reads the entirety of the model's weights, or in the case of a mixture of experts (MoE) models, their active parameters, from memory over and over again for each token generated. Because of this, how quickly an AI system can churn out tokens is directly proportional to how fast its memory is.

Prefill is comparatively write heavy, so it makes sense to do as much of that in HBM as possible. But the decode phase is almost entirely read, which makes HBF an ideal medium for storing model weights as write endurance really isn’t a factor.

It becomes a sort of write-once, read-many scenario, which is perfect for NAND flash since reads are essentially free. You could almost think about HBF a bit like a rewritable ROM cartridge for models. And because HBF is non-volatile, it becomes a bit like Intel’s Optane persistent memory. There is no need to wait for weights to reload from storage into GPU memory; they’re already there and ready to go.

Sandisk’s slides propose a couple of different options including one that would feature 3.12 TB of memory across two stacks of HBM and six stacks of HBF.

Oh the things you can do with all that memory

REG AD

That much memory has implications for model and inference architectures.

Most frontier models at this point employ a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, which means the model is really a collection of routed sub-models called experts, a small selection of which are used to generate each token.

This has allowed model devs to build models larger than would otherwise be practical to serve due to memory bandwidth constraints.

Because HBM’s capacity is so limited, these experts usually have to be spread across multiple GPUs connected by extremely high-speed interconnects. But with high-bandwidth flash, even multi-trillion-parameter models, like Kimi K3, could be packed into a single accelerator, mitigating any of the performance bottlenecks induced by the chip-to-chip interconnects.

On the flip side, HBF could allow a 72-GPU rack to run some truly massive models measuring hundreds of trillions of parameters.

Training such a model presents its own unique set of challenges, and the number of active experts/parameters would be limited by HBF’s bandwidth, but it could work.

So when?

So when can we expect to see HBF deployed in datacenters? If Sandisk is to be believed, the first samples should go out later this year with the first AI inference devices based on HBF available early next year.

But for a variety of reasons previously highlighted by our sibling site Blocks and Files, we’re not holding our breath.

One of the biggest factors is standardization. Memory is a commodity business and blazing your own trail with a proprietary technology rarely pans out — just look at Optane if you need evidence of that.

Sandisk and SK Hynix officially kicked off this process earlier this year under the auspices of the Open Compute Project.

“The key to AI infrastructure is to go beyond the performance competition of individual technologies and to optimize the entire ecosystem,” Ahn Hyun, president and chief development officer at SK Hynix, said at the time.

There are also manufacturing considerations to be made. HBF is going to require a lot more dies per module than your typical flash storage device. What’s more, from what we understand, the specific kind of NAND used to make these modules is different from the kind used to make SSDs and other flash storage.

Those modules will need to be copackaged with accelerators, which means SK Hynix and Sandisk will need to get buy-in from GPU and ASIC makers, which is going to take time. In fact, it wouldn’t be surprising for these modules to be ready years before the first chips designed to take advantage of them enter production.®

content_html_zh:
事实上，每个高端 GPU 和 AI 加速器都依赖于高带宽内存 (HBM)，它每秒可以以多个 TB 的速度整理数据，但只能达到千兆字节，模型通常需要在多个处理器之间共享。 然而，一种新兴的存储技术可能会改变这一现状，将加速器内存容量从数百 GB 提高到 TB。

这项技术被称为高带宽闪存 (HBF)，由 Sandisk 和 SK Hynix 开发，旨在以类似 HBM 的速度提供类似 SSD 的容量。

剥开 HBF 的层层

REG AD

从概念上讲，高带宽闪存看起来和听起来很像 HBM。 它是通过将多层（Sandisk 第一代模块为 16 层）内存堆叠在一起组装而成，从而提高了容量和带宽。 但 HBM 使用 DRAM，而 HBF 则旨在使用 NAND 闪存。

REG AD

Sandisk 声称其第一代高带宽闪存据称将实现高达 1.6 TB/s 的读取带宽 [PDF]，这使其比 HBM3e 快一点，但比 HBM4 慢得多，HBM4 已经达到每 12 高堆栈 2.5 TB/s。 未来几代 HBF 预计将带宽提高到 2 TB/s 以上，最终达到 3.2 TB/s。

虽然带宽使得 HBF 作为 HBM 的替代品很有趣，但它真正的技巧是容量。 Sandisk 表示，由于它是使用 NAND 构建的，因此每个芯片可以实现高达 256 GB 的容量，这意味着每个 16 高模块可实现 512 GB 的容量。 这是 AMD 和 Nvidia 最新加速器中使用的 HBM4 容量的 14 倍多。

继续保持相似之处，HBF 模块与 HBM 具有相似的封装要求，这意味着您可以使用台积电 (TSMC) 的 CoWoS 或英特尔 (Intel) 的 EMIB 和 Foveros 技术等先进封装技术将它们融合到 GPU 芯片上。 人工智能加速器没有什么特别奇特的。

此外，存储供应商预计这些模块的功耗或价格不会高于 HBM。 从比特/美元的角度来看，HBF 看起来是一个不错的选择。

如果这一切听起来有点好得令人难以置信，那是因为尽管 HBF 具有所有优势，但它也带来了一些相当重大的妥协。

NAND 仍然不是 DRAM

据我们了解，主要的权衡是写入耐久性和访问延迟。 HBF 的性能可能与纸面上的 HBM 类似，但它仍然使用 NAND，NAND 在磨损之前具有有限的写入耐久性，并且访问延迟以微秒为单位，而 DRAM 的访问延迟为数十纳秒。

如果您要将 HBM​​ 换成 HBF，它（可能）不会表现得很好，而且会很快磨损，使您的价值 50,000 多美元的 GPU 变成镇纸 - 对于需要更长使用寿命以适应超大规模的折旧计划的产品来说，这不是理想的选择。

REG AD

相反，Sandisk 和 SK Hynix 提议使用 HBF 来补充 HBM，以使推理更具成本效益。 HBM 处理所有写入密集型内容，而 HBF 则负责管道的读取密集型部分。

虽然我们将推理视为一项工作，但它实际上是许多工作的集合，大致可以分为两类，一类是计算密集型的，另一类是带宽限制的。

第一个阶段称为预填充，涉及标记化和嵌入提示，在一次大的前向传递中将它们馈送到模型中，生成用于跟踪状态的键值缓存，并输出第一个标记。

第二个称为“解码”，针对生成的每个标记，一遍又一遍地从内存中读取模型的全部权重，或者在混合专家 (MoE) 模型的情况下，读取其活动参数。 因此，人工智能系统产生代币的速度与其内存速度成正比。

预填充的写入量相对较大，因此在 HBM 中尽可能多地执行预填充是有意义的。 但解码阶段几乎完全被读取，这使得 HBF 成为存储模型权重的理想介质，因为写入耐久性实际上并不是一个因素。

它成为一种一次写入、多次读取的场景，这对于 NAND 闪存来说是完美的，因为读取基本上是免费的。 您几乎可以将 HBF 想象为模型的可重写 ROM 盒。 由于 HBF 是非易失性的，因此它有点像英特尔的 Optane 持久内存。 无需等待权重从存储重新加载到 GPU 内存；他们已经在那里并准备出发了。

Sandisk 的幻灯片提出了几种不同的选项，其中一种采用跨两个 HBM 堆栈和六个 HBF 堆栈的 3.12 TB 内存。

哦，你可以用所有的记忆来做一些事情

REG AD

这么多的内存对模型和推理架构都有影响。

目前大多数前沿模型都采用专家混合 (MoE) 架构，这意味着该模型实际上是称为专家的路由子模型的集合，其中一小部分用于生成每个令牌。

这使得模型开发人员能够构建比由于内存带宽限制而实际可用的模型更大的模型。

由于 HBM 的容量非常有限，这些专家通常必须分布在通过极高速互连连接的多个 GPU 上。 但有了高带宽闪存，即使是数万亿参数的模型（如 Kimi K3）也可以打包到单个加速器中，从而缓解芯片间互连引起的任何性能瓶颈。

另一方面，HBF 可以允许 72 个 GPU 机架运行一些测量数百万亿参数的真正大规模模型。

训练这样的模型面临着一系列独特的挑战，活跃专家/参数的数量将受到 HBF 带宽的限制，但它是可行的。

那么什么时候呢？

那么我们什么时候可以看到 HBF 部署在数据中心呢？ 如果 Sandisk 可信的话，第一批样品将于今年晚些时候推出，首款基于 HBF 的人工智能推理设备将于明年初上市。

但由于我们的兄弟网站 Blocks and Files 之前强调过的各种原因，我们并没有屏住呼吸。

最大的因素之一是标准化。 内存是一项商品业务，利用专有技术开拓自己的道路很少会成功——如果您需要这方面的证据，只需看看 Optane。

Sandisk 和 SK Hynix 今年早些时候在开放计算项目的支持下正式启动了这一进程。

SK 海力士总裁兼首席开发官 Ahn Hyun 当时表示：“人工智能基础设施的关键是超越单个技术的性能竞争，优化整个生态系统。”

还需要考虑制造因素。 与典型的闪存设备相比，HBF 每个模块需要更多的芯片。 更重要的是，据我们了解，用于制造这些模块的特定 NAND 类型与用于制造 SSD 和其他闪存存储的类型不同。

这些模块需要与加速器共同封装，这意味着 SK Hynix 和 Sandisk 需要获得 GPU 和 ASIC 制造商的支持，而这需要时间。 事实上，这些模块在第一批利用它们设计的芯片投入生产之前几年就已经准备就绪，这并不奇怪。®
